captions.instagram:
How does a fax machine work?

A fax turns your page into 2 million dots, squeezes them 10 to 20 times with a clever code book, and sings them down a phone line. Scan your own drawing, read the real run codes, hear the handshake, and watch line noise smear a page until error correction fixes it.

→ A fax machine is a scanner, a printer and a modem sharing one phone line.
→ The scanner reads one thin line at a time: 1,728 dots, each judged black or white.
→ Fine mode reads twice as many lines, and photos become patterns of tiny dots.
→ A fax sends runs, not dots: "312 white, 4 black", each turned into a short code.
→ The fax song is two modems talking: a beep, an answer tone, then a warble at 300 bits a second.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/faxclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a fax machine work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A fax turns your page into 2 million dots, squeezes them 10 to 20 times with a clever code book, and sings them down a phone line. Scan your own drawing, read the real run codes, hear the handshake, and watch line noise smear a page until error correction fixes it.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/faxclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/faxclear

In this video:
• Three machines in one box. A fax is a scanner, a modem and a printer sharing one phone line.
• A page becomes dots. The scanner reads one thin line at a time: 1,728 dots across 215 mm, about 204 per inch.
• Runs, not dots. Sending every dot at 9,600 bit/s would take over three minutes.
• The fax song. A phone line carries only sound, about 300–3,400 Hz.
• Printing, and fixing errors. The receiver decodes the runs and fires 1,728 heaters, one per dot, against paper that turns black at about 100 °C.
• Fax today. Over the internet, one lost packet can break the modem sound, so T.38 (1998) sends the fax data in packets with spare copies.
